question: Can a statistical-mechanics phase diagram, with SGD temperature set by learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio and disorder set by initialization variance, explain distinct neural-network training regimes and provide a usable hyperparameter boundary?

key_findings.claim: For mean-squared-error networks, the last hidden-layer features admit a disordered-soft-spin interpretation in which the output-layer Gram matrix supplies Wishart-like couplings, the labels supply an external field, bounded tanh activations are soft spins, and initialization variance controls disorder.
key_findings.evidence: The loss is algebraically decomposed into a quadratic feature interaction and a target-feature field term. For tanh features induced by approximately Gaussian preactivations, the effective feature potential changes from single-well to double-well when the preactivation variance crosses one half; large variance pushes activations toward saturation and small gradients. The output-weight Gram matrix has the stated Wishart mean and covariance at initialization.

key_findings.claim: A controlled tanh teacher-student experiment exhibits three qualitatively different regions: successful ordered learning, initialization-jammed learning, and noise-dominated high-temperature dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: Across a grid in T = learning rate / batch size and inverse initialization scale, low T with small initialization variance produces low test loss, small final gradient, strong target-feature alignment, and erased initial-feature memory. Large variance preserves initial-feature correlations and yields slow or ineffective training, while high T yields large loss and gradient and rapidly erases initialization memory. The grid uses 100 independently sampled teachers per point, 4,000 training and 100 test examples, and 100,000 SGD steps.

key_findings.claim: The singular-value dynamics of the trained middle layer separate the same regimes and motivate a one-dimensional stochastic description based on average eigenvalue spacing.
key_findings.evidence: For X = W(2)W(2)^T, the initially Marchenko-Pastur spectrum moves toward the teacher spectrum in the ordered regime, barely evolves from an extremely broad initial spectrum in the jammed regime, and spreads rapidly in the high-temperature regime. Starting from generalized Dyson Brownian motion, the paper subtracts the extreme-eigenvalue equations and approximates all spacings by their mean to obtain dS/dt = K_S + V_S T S + sqrt(2 T D_S) noise.

anchors.section: Stochastic dynamics of average level spacing

key_findings.claim: A drift-versus-noise stability inequality empirically tracks the high-temperature boundary, but it is primarily a retrospective diagnostic rather than a stand-alone prescriptive rule.
key_findings.evidence: Assuming K_S < 0 and V_S > 0 near a minimum, the deterministic spacing equation converges when T S is no larger than -K_S/V_S. Bounding the initial spacing with the Marchenko-Pastur support yields an inequality involving T/sigma_W^2 and the end-of-training gradient signal-to-noise ratio. Boundaries at 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of 100-run ensembles visually follow the feature-correlation and alignment transitions. The right-hand side, however, is measured after completing training.

key_findings.claim: The phase language is a useful organizing analogy, not yet evidence of thermodynamic phase transitions or a generally applicable neural-network tuning law.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly probe finite networks empirically rather than deriving a free energy or order parameters, and identify defining a suitable thermodynamic limit and finite-size scaling as future work. The sole main experiment is a 3-32-16-1 tanh regression network in which only the middle matrix is trained while the first and last matrices are copied from the teacher; realistic data, other activations, deeper/wider models, and all-layer dynamics are deferred.

method.core_idea: Translate MSE training into a disordered feature-space Hamiltonian, interpret mini-batch SGD as Langevin dynamics with effective temperature T = learning rate / batch size, and use the spectrum of a trainable weight Gram matrix to diagnose ordered, initialization-jammed, and high-temperature regimes.
method.mechanism: The tanh feature distribution supplies an initialization-controlled symmetry-breaking picture. A teacher-student sweep measures loss, gradient norm, feature memory, and target alignment. Separately, generalized Dyson Brownian motion for W W^T is reduced to a stochastic equation for the mean distance between its smallest and largest eigenvalues; comparing the restoring drift with stochastic eigenvalue repulsion yields an empirical convergence boundary.
assumptions: Mini-batch gradient fluctuations are sufficiently independent and approximately Gaussian for the discrete SGD update to admit the stated continuous-time Langevin description with T = learning rate / batch size.
The tanh preactivations are approximately Gaussian, and their variance is adequately controlled by the initialization variance used as the disorder axis.
The behavior of one trainable middle layer with teacher-matched surrounding layers is informative about multilayer neural-network optimization more broadly.
Replacing all eigenvalue gaps by a scaled average gap preserves the stability-relevant part of the coupled Dyson Brownian dynamics.
The end-of-training extreme-eigenvalue drift satisfies K_S < 0 and the derived Coulomb coefficient V_S is positive near the relevant solutions.
Finite-grid crossovers seen in ensembles of small networks meaningfully correspond to the ordered, paramagnetic, and spin-glass-like terminology used for thermodynamic systems.

techniques.role: Rewrites MSE into soft-spin interactions and a target-dependent external field.
Relates initialization variance to saturation, symmetry breaking, and gradient suppression.
Uses learning rate divided by batch size as the stochasticity coordinate of the phase diagram.
Creates a controlled target and measures 100 independent models at every grid point.
Distinguishes poor learning caused by frozen initialization from poor learning caused by strong noise.
Tracks squared singular values of the trainable matrix throughout optimization.
Compresses coupled stochastic eigenvalue dynamics into an approximate scalar SDE.
Classifies runs by comparing stochastic spreading with restoring gradient drift.

evaluations.setting: Tanh teacher-student regression with architecture 3-32-16-1; first and output matrices fixed to the teacher; only the 16x32 middle matrix trained; 4,000 Gaussian training inputs and 100 test inputs
evaluations.metric: Mean test MSE, full-data gradient norm, initial-to-final feature correlation, and normalized target-field/feature alignment after 100,000 iterations
evaluations.result: A low-temperature/small-variance region reaches losses near the low end of the reported roughly 10^-7 to 10^-1 range and high alignment; large variance retains initial memory; high temperature produces large loss and gradient independent of initialization.
evaluations.baseline: Other points in the same T by inverse-initialization-scale sweep; no standard optimizer-tuning baseline

evaluations.setting: The same 100-model ensembles at representative ordered, high-temperature, and jammed hyperparameters
evaluations.metric: Trajectories of all 16 eigenvalues of W(2)W(2)^T and final time-averaged logarithmic mean-spacing growth
evaluations.result: Ordered spectra approach teacher eigenvalues, high-temperature spectra expand rapidly, and jammed spectra start broad and move slowly; the spacing-rate heatmap qualitatively agrees with feature observables.
evaluations.baseline: Marchenko-Pastur spectrum at random initialization and the teacher spectrum

evaluations.setting: End-of-training stability classification over each 100-run hyperparameter ensemble
evaluations.metric: Fraction of models satisfying the derived mean-spacing convergence inequality at 68%, 95%, and 99.7% thresholds
evaluations.result: The inferred contours visually track the transition between ordered/jammed dynamics and the noise-dominated region, especially in the feature-memory heatmap.
evaluations.baseline: Empirical phase maps from loss, alignment, and feature correlation; no held-out architecture or prospective tuning test

limitations: The evidence comes from one very small synthetic tanh regression network; only one middle matrix is optimized, and the frozen surrounding matrices reveal the teacher's exact representation.

No experiments test ReLU-family activations, realistic datasets, classification, deeper or wider networks, simultaneous all-layer training, momentum, adaptive optimizers, weight decay, schedules, or modern architectures.

The temperature identification T = learning rate / batch size depends on a Langevin approximation whose assumptions can fail at the paper's very large discrete learning rates, with correlated mini-batch noise, or outside plain SGD.
The claimed phase boundaries are finite-size crossovers: there is no thermodynamic limit, free-energy calculation, conventional order parameter, critical exponent, or finite-size-scaling analysis.

Calling the large-variance region a spin glass or jamming phase is not supported by replica-symmetry breaking, metastable-state counting, aging tests, or other standard spin-glass diagnostics; ordinary tanh saturation and vanishing gradients can explain much of it.

The high-temperature boundary requires drift and gradient-variance quantities measured at the end of training, limiting its prospective utility for choosing hyperparameters before paying the training cost.
Mean extreme-eigenvalue spacing discards eigenvectors, internal spectral shape, feature geometry, and function-space behavior; similar spacing can coexist with very different models.

The advice to use the largest temperature inside the ordered region is not evaluated against random search, schedulers, learning-rate finders, early stopping, or wall-clock/sample-efficiency baselines.
failure_modes: With an unbounded or one-sided activation, the tanh double-well argument and vertical disorder boundary may disappear or change qualitatively.
When all layers learn, their coupled rescalings and symmetries can move spectra without changing the represented function, breaking the proposed spectral interpretation.
At finite step size, discrete updates can enter catapult or edge-of-stability dynamics that are not faithfully represented by the continuous Langevin equation.
Momentum, Adam, batch normalization, data augmentation, or nonstationary schedules can make a single scalar learning-rate-to-batch-size temperature inadequate.
The scalar spacing approximation can predict convergence even while interior eigenvalues, eigenvectors, or loss dynamics remain unstable.
An end-of-run boundary can look accurate by construction yet fail to forecast a new run, architecture, seed distribution, dataset, or training horizon.
A large-variance model may escape saturation on a longer time horizon, so fixed-step observations can conflate a slow crossover with a distinct phase.
reusable_insights: Use at least two observables to distinguish frozen poor learning from noise-driven poor learning; loss alone makes them look identical.
Track initialization memory and target alignment alongside gradients when diagnosing whether optimization is moving productively.
Treat spectral summaries as dynamical diagnostics and validate them against function-space metrics rather than assuming spectra determine learning.
Separate an analytically convenient effective temperature from the optimizer's actual noise covariance, which can be anisotropic and state dependent.
A claimed phase diagram should include prospective prediction on held-out architectures and finite-size scaling, not only retrospective contours on the data used to infer it.
Hyperparameter boundaries based on late-training statistics become more useful if early-time estimators or cheap probe runs can predict the same quantities.
When importing statistical-mechanics language, state which phenomena are exact algebraic correspondences, which are approximations, and which are only analogies.
open_questions: Does the three-region diagram survive simultaneous training of all layers on realistic datasets and ReLU, GELU, convolutional, residual, or transformer architectures?
Can early gradients, short probe trajectories, or initialization statistics predict K_S/V_S well enough to locate the boundary before a full training run?
What thermodynamic scaling of width, depth, learning rate, and parameterization preserves feature learning rather than collapsing to a lazy-training limit?
Do standard spin-glass diagnostics reveal a genuine glassy regime, or is the observed large-variance region simply activation saturation with long escape times?
How does the diagram change under momentum, Adam, learning-rate schedules, varying batch size, normalization, weight decay, and structured or heavy-tailed gradient noise?
Can a richer spectral state variable retain interior density and eigenvector information while remaining tractable enough for a predictive stability theory?
Does tuning just below a measured transition improve wall-clock convergence or generalization over modern automated learning-rate and batch-size selection methods?
How stable are the boundaries across training horizon, dataset size, teacher mismatch, label noise, and input dimension?

competitive_landscape.title: On the different regimes of Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Sclocchi and Wyart derive noise-dominated SGD, large-first-step SGD, and gradient-descent regimes in the batch-size/learning-rate plane for a teacher-student perceptron and test predictions in deep networks. The present paper instead varies initialization disorder and explains its regimes through bounded features and weight-spectrum dynamics, but validates only the small synthetic model.

competitive_landscape.title: The large learning rate phase of deep learning: the catapult mechanism
competitive_landscape.difference: The catapult work derives a stable nonlinear large-step regime and demonstrates it in practical networks, including movement toward flatter regions. The present Langevin-temperature picture treats large learning-rate behavior chiefly as stochastic spreading and does not isolate discrete-time catapult dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
competitive_landscape.difference: Edge-of-stability work measures the loss-Hessian maximum eigenvalue relative to 2/step size in realistic full-batch training. This paper instead studies eigenvalues of a weight Gram matrix under mini-batch noise and derives a drift/noise spacing condition; it does not compare the two boundaries.

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic weight matrix dynamics during learning and Dyson Brownian motion
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct methodological predecessor from the same research line
competitive_landscape.difference: The predecessor derives generalized Dyson Brownian motion for stochastic weight matrices and eigenvalue repulsion. The present paper's incremental contribution is to reduce that machinery to average spacing and combine it with a tanh initialization-disorder phase diagram and empirical boundary.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Information Propagation
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Information Propagation uses mean-field signal propagation to locate ordered/chaotic critical initialization and relate it to trainable depth. The present work varies initialization scale jointly with SGD noise and focuses on bounded-feature saturation and post-initialization weight spectra rather than propagation through deep random layers.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: the paper's distinctive synthesis is the two-axis diagram joining a tanh soft-spin initialization argument to an average-spacing reduction of Dyson Brownian weight dynamics. The individual ingredients are not new: SGD temperature, phase diagrams of optimization regimes, edge/catapult behavior, signal-propagation transitions, and random-matrix tracking all have substantial prior literature, and the Dyson framework is the authors' own earlier work. The synthesis is conceptually useful and produces a diagnostic contour in a controlled model, but the strongest practical and universality claims await prospective validation on modern all-layer training and a demonstrated separation from simpler saturation and stability explanations.
reviewer_notes: All 27 pages were reviewed, including the Hamiltonian mapping, initialization analysis, SGD approximation, complete experiment, every phase observable, spectral trajectories, scalar-SDE derivation, boundary construction, discussion, appendices, and references. Direct primary-source competitors were checked on arXiv on 2026-08-23. The review distinguishes the exact MSE algebra from the Gaussian/Langevin/mean-spacing approximations and from the paper's phase-language analogy. The released experiment is unusually reproducible in its grid and ensemble description, but the central boundary is evaluated with end-of-training quantities on the same narrow teacher-student setting used to motivate it.
